title: Trump's New Student Visa Rules Could Cost US Economy Up to $481 Billion a Year
excerpt: A Peterson Institute analysis warns that capping F-1 visas at four years and tightening oversight will shrink the STEM workforce and slow growth for a decade.
body:
• The Trump administration has ended the decades-old "duration of status" policy, capping student visas at four years with mandatory extensions through USCIS
  • F-1 visa issuance ran a third below normal through September 2025 after initial rule changes, with a further 22% drop in May 2025
  • The Peterson Institute estimates the crackdown could reduce annual GDP by $240 billion to $481 billion within a decade — equivalent to removing Wisconsin's entire economy
  • The rules take effect in September 2026, affecting roughly 1.2 million foreign students currently in the United States

The Trump administration's latest crackdown on international students could punch a hole in the US economy the size of Wisconsin, according to a new analysis that has alarmed educators, economists, and the Indian diaspora alike.

The Department of Homeland Security announced on July 16 that it would end the decades-old "duration of status" system, which allowed student, exchange, and media visa holders to remain in the United States for the length of their programs. Under the new rules, set to take effect in September, F-1 student visas will be capped at four years, with extensions requiring direct applications to US Citizenship and Immigration Services — complete with background checks, biometric screening, and fraud reviews.

The Economic Cost

A study by the Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE), authored by researcher Michael A. Clemens along with Amy Nice of Cornell University and Jeremy Neufeld of the Institute for Progress, estimates that within a decade annual GDP could be $240 billion to $481 billion lower than it would otherwise be.

The damage traces directly to the high-skill workforce. Some 35 percent of doctoral-level STEM workers in the United States are foreign-born and US-trained. F-1 visa issuance had already run approximately one-third below normal through September 2025 after an earlier round of restrictions, and fell 22 percent year-on-year in May 2025 alone.

"In comparable past episodes, neither foreign-trained workers from abroad nor U.S.-born students stepped in to fill the gap. We see no reason this time will be different."

— Michael A. Clemens, Peterson Institute for International Economics

What's Changing

The new rules affect three major visa categories: F visas for international students, J visas for exchange visitors, and I visas for foreign journalists. The post-graduation grace period for F-1 holders has been slashed from 60 days to 30. Current visa holders already in the country will be transitioned to the new framework, with their stays capped at four years from the rule's effective date.

Students from countries with visa overstay rates exceeding 10 percent, or those born in nations designated as state sponsors of terrorism, face even tighter limits — initial visas of just two years.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the changes, saying the "outdated 'duration of status' system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud."

Impact on Indian Students

India is the second-largest source of international students in the United States, and the policy change strikes at the heart of a migration pathway that tens of thousands of Indian families rely on each year. The four-year cap poses particular challenges for graduate and doctoral students in STEM fields, where programs frequently extend beyond that timeline.

The timing compounds existing pressures. The State Department paused student visa interviews between May 27 and June 18, 2025, during peak issuance season. When interviews resumed, they came with new requirements to vet applicants' social media accounts. Indian students have reported limited appointment availability at US consulates, creating backlogs that push planned enrolments back by semesters.

For families investing lakhs in American higher education, the calculus is shifting. Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom are positioning themselves as alternatives, and early data suggests students are listening — Canadian international enrolments have surged as America's global share of international students has fallen from nearly 30 percent in 2000 to roughly 16 percent today.

What's Next

The rule has been published in the Federal Register and takes effect 60 days after publication, placing the start date in September 2026. Legal challenges are widely expected. NAFSA, the Association of International Educators, has called the rule "complicated and burdensome," warning it would make it "far more difficult for international students and scholars to maintain their legal status."

Universities face their own reckoning. International students pay far higher tuition than domestic students and account for up to 30 percent of tuition revenue at some flagship public universities. With the administration simultaneously proposing cuts to the National Science Foundation and National Institutes of Health, the financial squeeze on American higher education could force painful trade-offs that ultimately hurt American students most.
